title: Technical Q&A, mid level software engineer, strong answers

questions.text: Walk me through how you would debug a service whose p99 latency doubled after a deploy.
How do you choose between a message queue and direct synchronous calls between services?
Explain database isolation levels, and when you would not use serializable.
How does a load balancer decide where to send a request?
Explain eventual consistency to a product manager.
How would you design rate limiting for a public API?

persona.pushback_style: asks why not the simpler option and tests the answer with a changed constraint

brief.curveball: Finance says to cut infrastructure cost by forty percent next quarter. Does the candidate's design change?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Imran, thanks for joining. I'm Dana, a staff engineer on the infrastructure team. This is a forty five minute technical conversation. Questions are spoken, with no coding, and I will push on your answers.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Sounds good, Dana. Thanks for having me.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What does your team own right now?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I'm on a payments platform team of six. We own the ledger service and the retry pipeline behind it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. I'll cover debugging, system design and data consistency, then leave time for your questions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Walk me through how you would debug a service whose p99 latency doubled after a deploy.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: First I confirm it is the deploy: I compare p99 before and after on the dashboard, and roll back if it is clearly tied to the release, because rollback is cheap. Then I split latency by endpoint and by dependency using traces. At my current job, p99 on the ledger service went from 180 to 400 milliseconds after a release. Traces showed a new database call inside a loop, 25 calls per request. I batched it into one query and p99 came back to 190.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Say rollback is not possible because of a schema change. What now?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Then I use a feature flag to turn off the new code path if one exists. If not, I ship a forward fix and limit risk by sending only 5 percent of requests to it first, watching p99 and error rate for 15 minutes before going wider. I also tell the on call engineer and the team channel, so people stop making unrelated changes while we investigate.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you choose between a message queue and direct synchronous calls between services?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I ask whether the caller needs the answer now. If the user is waiting on the result, a synchronous call is simpler. If the work can finish later, like sending a receipt or updating a report, I use a queue so a slow downstream service cannot slow the caller. We moved receipt sending to a queue last year, and checkout p99 fell from 900 to 350 milliseconds. The cost is more moving parts: retries, duplicate messages and harder tracing.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why not the simpler option? Direct calls with retries are easier to reason about.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: For many cases I agree, and I still use direct calls on the checkout path itself. But retries on a direct call extend the user's wait. When the receipt service was down for 20 minutes, checkout errors reached 12 percent before we moved it. With a queue, the receipts waited and checkout stayed healthy. So I choose by how much failure I can tolerate in the user path.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Suppose finance tells you to cut infrastructure cost by forty percent next quarter. Does your answer change?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The details change, not the principle. A managed queue is a running cost, so I would first check how many messages we send, and whether a database table with a worker, an outbox, could carry the low volume flows. For a flow under 50 messages a second, that is probably enough and costs nothing extra. I would keep the real queue only where volume or bursts justify it, and I would show finance the numbers.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Switching topics. When would you not use the serializable isolation level?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Serializable gives the strongest guarantee, but it costs throughput and can abort transactions that must be retried. I avoid it for hot rows, like a counter or an account balance updated by many requests, because conflicts rise sharply. For those I use a row lock or a single atomic update. I use serializable for rare, complex rules across several rows where a bug costs money, and I accept the retry logic. On our ledger, moving one hot path to row locks cut aborts from about 8 percent to under 1.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How does your team decide which latency targets to enforce?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Each service owns a p99 target agreed with its main callers, and we review misses in a monthly meeting.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's all we have time for. Thanks Imran, the recruiter will follow up within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Dana. I enjoyed the questions.

notes: Strong for mid: own production examples with numbers. Handles the pushback and the cost curveball with trade-off reasoning.
